name: AEI Healthcare Portfolio VII DST
description:
This DST opportunity is tailored for accredited investors seeking a diversified, debt-free investment—whether through a 1031 exchange or direct cash purchase. The portfolio is comprised of three high-quality, net-leased outpatient healthcare clinics, each backed by the strong corporate credit from tenants operating within a resilient sector.

These assets reflect AEI's investment approach to target exclusive specialty-market assets secured through specialized industry relationships, focusing on properties with market rents and purpose-built designs for outpatient medical services. This strategy promotes tenant retention and supports long-term rent growth. The portfolio features mission-critical healthcare facilities in prime markets, backed by long-term net leases with contractual annual rent escalations.

With no debt encumbering the properties, this offering provides investors with the potential for added financial stability. It is designed to deliver steady, monthly distributions through durable, high-demand outpatient healthcare real estate ownership.
notes:
The lack of mortgage debt reduces balance-sheet risk, but the key credit is the affiliated Master Tenant rather than the healthcare occupiers alone. The Master Tenant is newly formed, capitalized by a $500,000 demand note from AEI Trust Advisors that AEI Capital Corporation guarantees. The PPM states AEI and its affiliates have limited capital and no obligation to fund Master Lease shortfalls from other sources. This is a limited-credit Master Lease, not a corporate guaranty of the projected 5.00%-6.14% cash-flow schedule.

The portfolio combines new healthcare facilities with tenant concentration: Bristol represents 44.15% of Trust purchase price, Surprise 31.90%, and Austin 23.95%. The Master Lease captures property upside for the Master Tenant while the Trust bears specified Trust obligations and must depend on a Springing LLC if the Master Tenant defaults. The 721 route is not an investor-controlled liquidity right; it requires Trust Manager action and a Holder election.
cfDisclosure: PPM provides a 10-year investor distribution forecast: 5.00% in Year 1 to 6.14% in Year 10.

description:

The Parent Trust indirectly owns three self-storage properties located in the Phoenix, Arizona Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA), Dallas, Texas MSA and Orlando, Florida MSA. The Properties are operated by a subsidiary of SmartStop® Self Storage REIT (“SmartStop”) (NYSE:SMA) under the SmartStop Self Storage brand and operational platform.

The Parent Trust is offering (the Offering) to sell up to $28,444,976 of beneficial Interests to certain qualified, accredited Investors. The Offering is designed for Investors seeking to participate in a Section 1031 Exchange and those seeking to invest in self-storage assets.

[Portfolio size per the PPM: 1,927 storage units plus 12 vehicle storage spaces and 24 modular outdoor storage units (1,963 total spaces) and 222,296 net rentable square feet. The capital structure is the primary underwriting constraint: $24.19 million of interest-only debt equals 45.96% of total capitalization and matures in November 2032. The portfolio must either refinance, sell, or satisfy extension conditions at maturity; up to two one-year extensions reprice at SOFR + 150 bps. The 5.00% fixed coupon protects near-term debt service but creates a refinancing and valuation test at the balloon date.

Cash flow to investors is residual after lender-directed base rent. The Master Tenants are affiliated, limited-capital entities; they may retain part of upside but must cover operating shortfalls. Consequently, operating metrics at Phoenix, Longwood, and Dallas—not merely the stated 4.00%-4.25% distribution target—drive debt coverage and equity return. cfDisclosure: PPM Projected DST Cashflow: 6.10%, 6.38%, 6.69%, 7.00%, 7.31%, 7.62%, 7.96% in Years 1-7. The schedule ends at the seven-year loan maturity; Years 8-10 are not 0%.
sourceNotes:
BREX Net Lease Industrial I DST - Delaware Statutory Trust Program Memorandum and Property Supplement both dated 4/17/2026, plus the April 2026 Offering Summary brochure, retrieved from the Baker1031 Team Folder on Dropbox and verified against Dropbox content hashes. Single asset, single tenant. The Trust closed the acquisition on 3/23/2026, buying from DIV BMT, LLC, an unaffiliated third-party seller, for $155.4MM against a Capright appraisal of $158.0MM as of 2/28/2026 - a 1.65% discount to appraised value, and no depositor markup: the price in the Estimated Use of Proceeds table is the price paid to the seller. Leveraged: $84.0MM from PNC Bank, N.A., also unaffiliated.

BREX LTV basis. The 51.20% shown is the sponsor's own fully-loaded loan-to-capitalization ratio, debt over debt plus equity ($164,055,365). This offering is the only one in the workbook that spells out the identification worksheet arithmetic directly: the minimum purchase is $100,000 of equity plus $104,927 of debt for a 0.1249% interest, and the PPM states each Purchaser should be deemed to have assumed $104,927 of mortgage debt per 0.1249% interest. That implied ratio is 51.2021%, matching the 51.2022% computed here to four decimals. Against the $155.4MM property purchase price the ratio is 54.05%. The PPM adds its own caution that the ratio 'should not be assumed as dispositive for purposes of determining any debt-relief boot'.

BREX interest rate is not simply fixed, and this is the only offering in the workbook where that is true. The underlying Loan is variable at Compounded SOFR + 1.45% for its full 7-year term. A Hedge converts it to an effective fixed 4.837% only through the fifth anniversary. The Loan Documents require the Hedge to be extended or replaced with an economically equivalent hedge through maturity, but that replacement does not exist yet and its cost is unknown. The Exhibit C forecast nevertheless runs 4.837% through years 6 and 7, so the last two years of projected distributions rest on a hedge assumption rather than a contract. Debt service reconciles exactly on an actual/360 basis: $84.0MM x 4.837% x 365/360 = $4,119,512 in ordinary years and x 366/360 = $4,130,798 in the two leap years, matching the printed figures to the dollar.

BREX cash flow runs seven years, not ten, because the Loan matures in year 7 - Yr 8-10 are deliberately blank and Average Cash Flow for this row is the 7-year average of 7.01%. Percentages are the printed Cash-on-Cash Return line of Exhibit C, Projected DST Cashflow. Each one recomputes from the underlying dollars against the $80,055,365 equity to within 0.3 bps, and Base Rent less Total Trust Fees and Expenses reproduces Projected Distributions on all seven years to within $1.

The seven-year cliff - the most important disclosure in this offering. The Loan matures 3/23/2033. The Property Supplement states that if by then the Manager has not sold the Property and the Operating Partnership has not exercised its FMV Option, the Trust must refinance or raise capital from Beneficial Owners - but that the Trust, as a fixed investment trust, is prohibited from doing either, so 'the Manager will be required to effectuate a Transfer Distribution in order to pursue these options and avoid a default under the Loan.' A Transfer Distribution converts the Trust to an LLC taxed as a partnership, at which point the investor holds a partnership interest rather than real property and cannot complete a subsequent Section 1031 exchange. So the structure has exactly three seven-year outcomes: a sale, a sponsor-elected 721, or a springing-LLC conversion that forecloses the 1031. Note also that the Base Rent table for Years 8-20 is expressly premised on the Loan being repaid with additional capital raised from Beneficial Owners.

BREX 721 exit is the most one-sided of the six and 'Optional' understates it. The Operating Partnership - not the investor - decides whether to exercise the FMV Option at all, and may not exercise it before a two-year hold. If it does exercise, the PPM states the Operating Partnership 'has the sole discretion to acquire a Beneficial Owner's interest in the Trust for cash rather than exchange such interest for OP Units' and, 'for the avoidance of doubt, the Operating Partnership has the sole discretion to determine a Cash Investor and not all Beneficial Owners may become a Cash Investor.' The investor therefore has no election either way. Compare: ExchangeRight gives an investor-elected menu of five; Bluerock defaults to OP Units but lets the investor elect cash within 20 business days for a 2% fee; Blue Door lets the investor elect if the trustee undertakes an OP Transaction; AEI defaults to cash at the manager's discretion. BREX alone gives the investor nothing to elect. Timing compounds it: OP Units are delivered within 60 business days of the Receipt Date but cash within 180 business days - roughly nine months - which will not fit inside the 45-day identification and 180-day closing windows of a subsequent exchange.

BREX front-end load is the lowest in the workbook, on the same itemized basis as the others: selling commissions $4,002,768 (5.00%), dealer manager fee $800,554 (1.00%), placement fee $800,554 (1.00%) and O&O $400,277 (0.50%) = $6,004,152, which is 7.50% of the $80,055,365 equity and 3.66% of total capitalization. There is no acquisition fee - the only offering of the six without one. Compare ExchangeRight 9.21%, AEI 9.12%, Blue Door 15.19%, BR Parkview 13.67%. Separate transaction costs of $2,651,213 (reserves $1.0MM, loan fees and costs $1,250,936, property closing costs $400,277) are not sponsor compensation. The full table cross-foots to $164,055,365 within $1. Ongoing fees are an Investor Servicing Fee of 0.25% and an Administration Fee of 0.15% of equity annually, plus a 2.0%-of-gross-revenues Property Management Fee paid by the Master Tenant.

BREX has the strongest Master-lease credit of the six. Percentages are Exhibit A's 'Estimated Levered Cashflow Yield on Offering Equity'. Averaged over the seven years the two measures are 4.59% (hypothetical) against 4.14% (cash).

CF Biscayne's Master lease is fixed rent only - no percentage rent, no additional rent, no bonus rent. The PPM states the Master Tenant's obligation 'is limited to the Fixed Rent and the Master Tenant is entitled to retain any other revenues generated by the Property after payment of Fixed Rent.' Year-over-year growth runs +4.96%, -0.14%, +0.01%, +0.01%, +8.86%, +1.12%, tracking debt service so that the distribution lands exactly on 4.30% and then 3.75%. name: ExchangeRight Net-Leased All-Cash 21 DST
description:
ExchangeRight Net-Leased All-Cash 21 DST is a debt-free offering of net-leased real estate backed by historically recession-resilient tenants, with a 5.05% current cash flow from in-place lease revenue. The portfolio is focused on properties that are leased to national tenants successfully operating in necessity-based industries.

ExchangeRight is offering up to 100% of the beneficial interests in the DST to accredited investors. The Offering is designed for investors seeking to participate in a 1031 tax-deferred exchange as well as investors seeking a net-leased real estate investment on a cash basis. Though offering objectives and pro forma are based on contractual rent obligations, there is no guarantee that this offering will meet its investment objectives.
notes:
The underwriting is principally a platform-credit thesis rather than a conventional six-asset real-estate thesis. The Master Lessee and Manager are ExchangeRight affiliates; the PPM states the Master Lease was not negotiated at arm’s length. The Trust’s sole pre-disposition income source is fixed Master Lease rent, and the guarantor is ExchangeRight Income Fund Operating Partnership, LP. Investor cash flow therefore depends on that affiliated guarantor’s liquidity, balance-sheet capacity, and ability to fund obligations—not merely on the property-level performance of Lowe’s, Hobby Lobby, Dollar Tree, and Novant Health.

FSX Industrial 35, DST - PPM dated 7/7/2026 (185 pp.) plus the term sheet and an independent Orgill credit report, all three retrieved from the Baker1031 Team Folder on Dropbox and verified against Dropbox content hashes. From the Alliance Group credit report bound into the package, EBITDA has fallen from $221 million in 2023 to $185 million in 2024 to $151 million in 2025 - down 32% from the peak and the lowest margin of the six-year review period, which the analyst attributes partly to tariffs. Two FSX document items to raise with the Sponsor. (a) The liquidity figures conflict. Each Holder grants the Parent Trust Manager (or its assign) “the right, but not the obligation, to require that each Holder exchange its Interest in the Parent Trust for limited liability company or limited partner interests in the Exchange Entity” in a transaction intended to qualify under Code Section 721. The Parent Trust Manager “has the right to assign the Exchange Right to another entity, including an entity that is managed or sponsored by the Parent Trust Manager, the Sponsor or an Affiliate, but which the Parent Trust Manager expects will be the operating partnership of a REIT.” That is weaker than every other NexPoint offering in this workbook: Oasis names NXDT’s operating partnership outright, Life Sciences III at least confines the Exchange Entity to entities Controlled by NexPoint, and here the receiving vehicle is an expectation about an assignable right. Cash route: the PPM’s summary describes no cash election at all - unlike Oasis, Marina and Life Sciences III, each of which expressly lets a Holder elect cash instead of Units. Read the Parent Trust Agreement itself before representing that a cash alternative exists here.
highlights: No 1031 Investor can close until a “conversion notice” becomes effective, and the PPM never says when that is. “No purchase requests for Interests will be closed unless and until the effective date of the Conversion Notice … and the Parent Trust has been converted into an investment trust.” Counsel’s opinion is expressly conditioned on it: only “after the effective date of the Conversion Notice” should the Parent Trust and Subtrusts be treated as investment trusts under Treasury Regulations 301.7701-4(c)(1) and the Holders as owning an undivided beneficial interest in the Properties for Section 1031 purposes. The Offering Termination Date itself runs from “the first anniversary of the effective date of the Conversion Notice.” Nothing in the document states that the Conversion Notice has been delivered - every reference is prospective. This is the first question to ask the Sponsor: has the Conversion Notice gone effective, and on what date? Until it has, this is not a placeable 1031 offering.

The $4,062,000 PIP reserve is a promissory note from a Sponsor affiliate, and it was 40% funded at the PPM date. Both hotels must complete an extensive PIP within 18 months of their franchise agreements. The Riverfront PIP is estimated at approximately $4,062,000 - and rather than contribute cash, the Depositor contributed the “Riverfront Reserve Note” in exactly that amount “in lieu of contributing cash for the reserves.” It is an installment note: 5 monthly payments of $812,400 beginning 1 May 2026, guaranteed by OSL Holdco, another affiliate. The PPM states “As of the date of the Memorandum, we have funded $1,624,800” - two of five payments, leaving $2,437,200 unfunded, and the note “represents the majority of the Trust Reserves to be held by the Riverfront Subtrust.” So the money for a mandatory, franchisor-required PIP sits outside the trust as an unsecured affiliate obligation. Failure to complete a PIP is a franchise default, and a franchise default on a hotel can cost the flag. Ask for proof that payments 3, 4 and 5 have been made. By contrast Glastonbury’s $2,000,000 capital and $1,500,000 operating reserves are cash - the two hotels are funded on different terms.

The FF&E reserve ramps 0% / 2% / 5%, and that ramp is worth nearly a point on the year 1 headline. The DST bears the FF&E reserve as an expense before distributions. The exhibit takes nothing in year 1, 2.000% of hotel revenue in year 2, and 5.000% from year 3 on - all three verified exactly against the revenue line. Applying the sponsor’s own steady-state 5% to years 1 and 2 costs $766,257 and $499,845 - $1,266,103 in total - and restates the yield from 6.30% to 5.36% in year 1 (-0.94 points) and from 6.50% to 5.89% in year 2 (-0.61 points). For a hotel that is simultaneously undertaking two extensive PIPs, taking no FF&E reserve in year 1 is the assumption to interrogate first. Years 3-8 are unaffected.

The Master Tenants’ cushion is 3.9% to 7.8% of hotel EBITDA - thinnest in year 3. Rent absorbs 92% to 96% of forecast EBITDA: year 1 EBITDA $6,585,557 against rent of $6,218,404 leaves $367,154; year 3 EBITDA $8,366,147 against $8,041,489 leaves $324,658, which is 3.88% of EBITDA and just 1.78% of hotel revenue. A hotel is an operating business whose revenue moves several points in a soft year, and each Master Tenant was capitalised with $290,000 of operating reserves out of the $974,109 the Depositor pushed down. So roughly $6.2 million of year 1 rent is supported by a newly formed entity holding $290,000 of cash plus a $367,154 forecast margin. Mitigant worth weighing: the PPM discloses that the Ohio State Life Insurance Company - founded 1906, regulated by the Texas Department of Insurance, licensed in 46 states, rated B+ (Good) by AM Best - is the indirect owner of the Depositor and both Master Tenants, and is “indirectly controlled by a trust that also indirectly controls the NexPoint companies.” Indirect ownership is not a guarantee, and B+ is in AM Best’s “Good” band, not “Excellent” or “Superior.” Ask whether Ohio State Life guarantees either Master Lease. The PIP note is guaranteed by OSL Holdco, so the sponsor group does give guarantees when it chooses to.

Pricing, which looks worse than it is, and the franchise terms. The $81,573,000 offering price is 31.68% above the $61,950,000 combined purchase price - the widest gap in this workbook on that measure - but purchase price is the wrong denominator here because the structure carries $8,932,000 of reserves (10.95% of equity). The Depositor’s disclosed basis is $70,882,000 ($33,132,000 Riverfront including the $4,062,000 note, $37,750,000 Glastonbury), the offering is 15.08% above that, and above the Depositor’s all-in basis including every cost line ($80,598,891) the offering price is just +1.21% - the tightest of the three NexPoint offerings reviewed together. The whole waterfall reconciles to the dollar: $81,573,000 less $70,882,000 is $10,691,000, less Selling Commissions and Expenses $7,137,638 (8.75%), organization and offering $489,438 (0.60%), closing and due diligence $850,815 (1.04%) and the Facilitation Fee $1,239,000 (exactly 2.00% of purchase price) leaves $974,109, which is precisely the amount pushed down to the two Master Tenants. Front-end load 11.91% of equity. Adjust for the $2,437,200 of unfunded note and the all-in premium becomes +4.36%. Franchise: Glastonbury’s Hilton agreement is a 15-year non-renewable term, and for both hotels “neither the Subtrust nor the Parent Trust have any rights to the license” - the flag belongs to the Master Tenant, not to the asset the investor owns. Ground lease (Riverfront): 99 years from 23 April 1980, expiring 23 April 2079, so 53 years remain, renewable for a further 99 - and per a Ground Lessor Estoppel dated 11 March 2026 the City certified the rent “has been paid in full, and no rent is due or payable.” A prepaid 53-year leasehold clears the 30-year like-kind threshold comfortably, but title to the buildings and all FF&E passes to the City at expiration or earlier termination, and assignment needs the City’s consent.

name: NexPoint Marina DST
description:
NexPoint Marina DST is a Parent Trust owning 100% of the Class 2 Beneficial Interests in two Operating Trusts, each holding one multi-tenant marina and boatyard facility. All-cash, no financing. 711 boat slips plus 33 jet ski slips across the two properties.

Eufaula Cove Marina. 400 & 610 Lakeshore Drive, Eufaula, Oklahoma, on Lake Eufaula - approximately 145 acres, 459 slips, eight jet ski slips and roughly 14,200 net rentable SF of related amenities, developed 1988 and 2010. Occupancy was approximately 80% at 31 December 2025, which the PPM attributes to the seasonality of existing leases. Acquired 9 January 2026 for $25,000,000.

Grafton Harbor. 215 West Water Street, Grafton, Illinois, on the Mississippi River - approximately 5.48 acres, 252 slips, 25 jet ski slips and roughly 5,000 net rentable SF, developed 2006. “Structurally full, operating at effectively 100% occupancy with an active waitlist” at 16 February 2026. Acquired 9 January 2026 for $11,000,000.

Both properties are managed by New Haven Marinas, LLC, and each is master-leased to a separate sponsor-affiliated Master Tenant that subleases slips to end users and either subleases or directly operates on-site commercial businesses which at Eufaula may include a gas station and a restaurant.
notes: The all-cash capital stack supports the stated first-year 7.01% distribution objective, but marine operations introduce seasonal demand, water-level, weather, flood and municipal-lease risks. The legal ownership structure is also narrower than a typical fee-simple portfolio: key interests are leasehold rights and improvements, while certain personal property was assigned to the Master Tenants. The Master Tenants' small demand-note capitalization makes property cash flow and sponsor support material.
addresses: 400 & 610 Lakeshore Drive, Eufaula, OK 74432 (Eufaula Cove Marina, 459 slips + 8 jet ski slips, ~145 acres, ~14,200 NRSF, City leasehold to 1/1/2071); 215 West Water Street, Grafton, IL 62037 (Grafton Harbor, 252 slips + 25 jet ski slips, ~5.48 acres, ~5,000 NRSF, City leasehold to 8/17/2100)
sourceNotes: All disclosures and source notes for this offering are carried in the Highlight 1-5 columns and in the 721 Exit column of this row. Interest rate: none - the offering is all-cash with no financing. The "11/1/2032" maturity printed in the summary box is template residue. Minimum purchase: $100,000 of equity, a 0.234% Interest; no debt attributed.
numTenants: N/A - multi-tenant marinas (711 slips + 33 jet ski slips), each master-leased
walt: N/A - seasonal slip leases; City leaseholds run to 2071 and 2100
exit721Route: Sponsor-side right, unnamed recipient, and it can be exercised on one marina without the other. Beneficial Owners grant the “Exchange Entity” - defined only as “the Manager, its affiliates, successors, or assigns,” with not even the “Controlled by NexPoint” qualifier Life Sciences III carries - the right, but not the obligation, to require each Beneficial Owner to exchange for units or to have their Interests purchased for cash. Exercise requires a one-year hold. Fair market value is set by an independent appraisal the Manager selects in its sole discretion. Facilitation fees up to 4.0% of the owner’s investment. Unique to this Offering: “The Exchange Entity may exercise its Exchange Right at the Parent Trust level or at the operating Trust level” - so it can take Eufaula and leave Grafton, or the reverse, and if it exercises on one or more Operating Trusts the value is the sum of the fair market values of those Operating Trusts. NexPoint Small Bay III (row 18) carries the identical asset-level right - these two are the only offerings in this workbook that permit a partial, single-asset 721. Cash route: available as an election, no cap and no redemption fee disclosed. Once exercised, “you will not be able to engage in a subsequent, individual Section 1031 Exchange.”
highlights: What the Trusts actually own is not fee Real Estate, and this is the first thing to understand. The PPM defines a “Section 1031 Corpus” for each marina. At Eufaula it is (1) ownership of “certain improvements only (and not any underlying Real Estate or waters)” constructed upon the property and the waters of Lake Eufaula, plus (2) the leasehold interest under a lease from the City of Eufaula. At Grafton it is (1) fee simple in certain ancillary real estate adjacent to the marina - which the PPM says is “unrelated to and do[es] not impact the business operations” - plus (2) improvements only, not the underlying real estate or the waters of the Mississippi River, plus (3) the leasehold under a lease from the City of Grafton. Personal property and intangibles, including a Camp Jellystone franchise agreement at Eufaula, were assigned away to the Master Tenants and are expressly not part of the 1031 corpus - which is the right structuring, because personal property has not been 1031-eligible since the 2017 Act. Lease terms, which is what makes it work: the Eufaula City Lease runs to 1 January 2071 (about 45 years from the PPM date, with one 50-year renewal) and the Grafton City Lease to 17 August 2100 (about 74 years, with one 98-year renewal). Both clear the 30-year threshold at which a leasehold is treated as like-kind to a fee interest, comfortably, even after a ten-year hold. But note the landlords are municipalities, and a buyer in year 10 is buying a ~35-year Eufaula leasehold rather than land. Have counsel confirm the like-kind analysis before placing an exchange - this is the most structurally unusual corpus in this workbook.

$915,000 of the years 1-3 distributions is funded by the Investors’ own Offering proceeds, not Property cash flow. The forecast pays Base Rent to the Trust that includes an amount equal to the “Value-Add CapEx” spend ($290,000 / $300,000 / $325,000 in years 1-3) and distributes it, while the separate $915,000 CapEx Reserve - funded out of Offering Proceeds - actually pays for the work, running 915,000 to 625,000 to 325,000 to zero. From year 4 the exhibit deducts a “Reserve Contribution from Cash Flow” that exactly matches recurring capital improvements, so years 4-10 are self-funding. Testing distributions against NOI less all capital spending less the Master Tenant’s income less DST expenses and the asset management fee: years 4 through 10 balance to the dollar, and years 1-3 are short by exactly $290,000, $299,999 and $325,000 - a cumulative $914,999 against a $915,000 reserve. Restating those years: 7.01% becomes 6.33%, 7.26% becomes 6.56%, 7.45% becomes 6.69%. The 7.976% ten-year average is still the highest in this workbook, but the first three years are 0.68 to 0.76 points softer than printed.

The asset management fee is the plug that keeps the additional rent tier flat - the same construction as NexPoint Oasis. The exhibit shows an “Additional Rent Maximum” of $2,214,000 / $2,250,000 / $2,322,000 / $2,250,000 / $2,250,000 / $2,286,000 / $2,322,000 x 4, and the Asset Management Fee of $0 / $36,000 / $108,000 / $36,000 / $36,000 / $72,000 / $108,000 x 4. In all ten years the Maximum equals $2,214,000 plus the fee exactly, so the Additional Rent reaching investors is constant at $2,214,000 = 5.1838% of equity forever, and the “maximum” line is not a rent forecast at all - it is $2,214,000 plus the fee schedule. Note the series is not monotonic (it falls from $2,322,000 in year 3 to $2,250,000 in year 4), which is what proves the fee is driving it rather than property performance. Investor growth therefore comes entirely from the Supplemental Rent tier, which is genuinely revenue-driven: the Master Tenant takes 10% of Effective Gross Revenue above a Supplemental Breakpoint and the Trust takes 90%, and that reconciles against revenue less breakpoint within about $40 a year on a monthly basis. NexPoint Oasis does exactly the same thing at $1,748,000. Treat this as a structural feature of the sponsor’s master leases, not a quirk of one deal.

The “effective tax equivalent yield” row is computed by a formula with no economic meaning, and it overstates by up to 3.11 points. In all ten years the exhibit’s “Yield Net of Tax Benefit” equals estimated taxable income multiplied by 1.37 - not distributions less tax. Marina is all-cash, so there is no interest deduction and the forecast shows positive taxable income every year ($1,710,900 rising to $2,861,302); the sponsor’s template was built for the usual DST case where taxable income is a loss and the tax line is a refund to be added back, and applying it to positive income produces a number that is not a cash flow. Restated properly as (distributions less tax) over equity, divided by 0.63: year 1 is 8.77% against 8.71% printed, but by year 10 it is 11.46% against 14.57% printed. Ten-year average 9.74% restated against 10.82% printed. The whole tax chain is otherwise correct - 0.37 x taxable income reproduces the stated tax to the dollar in every year - so this is one bad row, not a bad model. For a non-1031 buyer the real point is that roughly 57% of the year 1 distribution is taxable ($1,710,900 of $2,992,203): there is very little depreciation shelter here, because the depreciable base is $32,400,000 of improvements against $42,710,095 of equity and there is no debt. 1031 purchasers carry over basis and are unaffected. Not tax advice - have this confirmed.

Pricing, appraisals and the fee load. $42,710,095 of equity against a $36,000,000 combined purchase price is +18.64%, and against purchase plus closing costs and the contribution fee ($37,366,701) it is +14.30%. The Contribution Fee of $720,000 is exactly 2.00% of purchase price - double the 1.00% on Life Sciences III - and the front-end load is 11.04% of equity. Every fee percentage and the whole use-of-proceeds table reconcile to the dollar, and the $1,350,000 of reserves foots exactly to its three components ($915,000 CapEx, $200,000 seasonal, $235,000 working capital). Appraisals: JLL valued Eufaula at $25,300,000 on 20 February 2026 and Grafton at $11,200,000 - but the Grafton appraisal is dated 16 February 2025, more than a year before the 2 March 2026 offering, where every other appraisal across these NexPoint offerings was struck within weeks of closing. Combined appraised value $36,500,000, so the purchase was 1.37% below appraisal and the offering price is 17.01% above it. Confirm whether the Grafton date is a typo or a genuinely year-old valuation. Template residue worth knowing about: the Investment Summary box prints “Maturity Date November 1, 2032” and “Interest Only Term 120 months” beside a Mortgage Principal of $0 and an Interest Rate of 0.00% - there is no loan, and 1 November 2032 is the maturity date of the NexPoint Life Sciences III loan. The printed 7.19% capitalisation rate also does not reproduce: NOI $3,069,011 over the $42,710,095 the box itself labels “Offering Price Less Reserves” is 7.18%, and net of the $1,350,000 of reserves the footnote describes it would be 7.42%. Seasonality is the operating risk the numbers do not show: these are Oklahoma and Illinois marinas paying monthly distributions, and Eufaula was 80% occupied at year end for exactly that reason.

name: NexPoint Marina II DST
description:
NexPoint Marina II DST is a Parent Trust owning 100% of the Class 2 Beneficial Interests in two Operating Trusts, each holding one marina. All-cash, no financing. 1,007 slips across approximately 80.1 acres of upland and submerged land, with roughly 12,637 net rentable square feet of related amenities.

Kuttawa Harbor Marina. 1709 Lake Barkley Drive, Kuttawa, Kentucky, on the Cumberland River - approximately 25.14 acres, 409 slips, ~5,281 NRSF, developed 1973 and 2011. Occupancy 100% at 30 June 2026. Operated under a lease from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers expiring 6 August 2050.

Stardust Marina. 149 Stardust Lane, Andersonville, Tennessee, on the Clinch River near the entrance to Norris Lake - approximately 54.96 acres, 598 slips, campground sites, ~7,356 NRSF, developed 1962, 1982, 2000 and 2004. Occupancy 85% at 30 June 2026 “due to the continued lease-up of new slips; prior to the addition of such slips, occupancy was approximately 95%.” Operated under a Tennessee Valley Authority licence that is terminable by either party on not less than 30 days’ notice, with scheduled licence payments contemplated through 2043. The Master Tenant is pursuing a 30-year TVA easement that would replace it.

Both properties are managed by New Haven Property Management, LLC and master-leased to sponsor-affiliated Master Tenants. On-site operations include fuel, dining, retail and boat rental.
addresses: 1709 Lake Barkley Drive, Kuttawa, KY 42055 (Kuttawa Harbor Marina - 409 slips, ~25.14 acres, ~5,281 NRSF, USACE lease to 8/6/2050 held by the MASTER TENANT); 149 Stardust Lane, Andersonville, TN 37705 (Stardust Marina - 598 slips plus campground, ~54.96 acres, ~7,356 NRSF, TVA licence terminable on 30 days' notice, held by the MASTER TENANT)
sourceNotes: All disclosures and source notes for this offering are carried in the Highlight 1-5 columns and in the 721 Exit column of this row. Minimum purchase: $100,000 of equity, a 0.204% Interest; no debt attributed.
numTenants: N/A - multi-tenant marinas (1,007 slips: 409 Kuttawa + 598 Stardust), 100% and 85% occupied
walt: N/A - seasonal slip leases. Government rights held by the Master Tenants, not the DSTs
exit721Route: Identical wording to NexPoint Marina I, and the same asset-level right. The “Exchange Entity” is defined only as “the Manager, its affiliates, successors, or assigns” - no “Controlled by NexPoint” qualifier, no named operating partnership - with the right, but not the obligation, to require each Beneficial Owner to exchange for units or to have their Interests purchased for cash. As with Marina I and Small Bay III, “the Exchange Entity may exercise its Exchange Right at the Parent Trust level or at the Operating Trust level,” so Kuttawa and Stardust can be taken separately. Fair market value by an independent appraisal the Manager selects; facilitation fees up to 4.0% of the owner’s investment; one-year hold before exercise. Cash route: available as an election, with no cap and no redemption fee disclosed. But note what would actually be exchanged here. The Operating Trusts own the improvements only - not the underlying land or waters, and not the Government Leases. On an appraisal-based fair-market-value determination, the appraisals in this PPM value each marina as an integrated operating business and expressly “do not attribute value to the applicable Government Lease or other assets held by the Master Tenant.” So the valuation basis for a 721 or a cash election is the same mismatched basis flagged in the pricing highlight. Ask how the Exchange Entity would value improvements-only interests on exercise.
highlights: The 1031 corpus is improvements only - weaker than Marina I, and this is the first thing to resolve. The PPM states it in bold: “the Kuttawa DST only owns the Kuttawa 1031 Corpus and the Stardust DST only owns the Stardust 1031 Corpus … the operating Trusts are not parties to the Government leases.” Each corpus is “ownership of certain improvements only (and not any underlying land or waters)” - plus, at Stardust only, fee simple in ancillary adjacent real estate the PPM says is “unrelated to and do[es] not impact the business operations.” Compare Marina I (row 16), where each Operating Trust holds the improvements and the city leasehold, running to 2071 and 2100. Here the right to occupy the land is held by the Master Tenant, a sponsor affiliate, under (a) a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers lease expiring 6 August 2050 - 24 years out, and note that a leasehold with under 30 years remaining would not be like-kind to a fee interest if the DST held it, which it does not - and (b) a TVA licence terminable on 30 days’ notice by either party. Improvements are real property, so the like-kind character is arguable; the problem is economic as much as tax. If either Government right ends, the Trust owns improvements on land it has no right to occupy. The Sponsor pushes the question to the investor: “Each prospective Purchaser should seek the advice of a qualified tax advisor as to the implications of the Parent Trust’s ownership of the Section 1031 Corpus.” Get that advice in writing before placing an exchange. Not tax advice.

The appraisals do not value what the Trusts own, and they land exactly on the affiliate transfer price. For both properties the PPM says the appraisal “values the Property as an integrated operating Marina in a business and economic sense,” that “the DST’s legal ownership interests differ from the assets and rights comprising the marina as an operating business,” and that it “does not attribute value to the applicable Government Lease or other assets held by the Master Tenant.” So the appraised value covers more than the 1031 corpus being sold, and the premium of the $48,968,013 offering price over the $42,000,000 appraised value - +16.59% - is measured against the wrong asset. On the improvements-only interest actually conveyed, the premium is not quantifiable from this document. And the appraisals themselves: JLL valued Kuttawa at $17,500,000 on 16 July 2026 and Stardust at $24,500,000 on 15 July 2026 - which are exactly the prices the sponsor affiliates paid on 17 July 2026, one and two days later respectively. Combined $42,000,000, to the dollar. The appraisals validate the marked-up affiliate price, not the $40,000,000 third-party price paid six months earlier.

Two affiliate flips added $2,000,000 to the basis in six months - the second time this pattern appears in this workbook. On 16 January 2026 NexPoint SFR OP TRS, LLC, “an affiliate of the Sponsor,” bought the Kuttawa SPE for $16,500,000 and the Stardust SPE for $23,500,000 - $40,000,000 combined - from Windlass Marinas, LLC, a third party unaffiliated with the Sponsor (though an affiliate of the Property Manager). On 17 July 2026 those interests were sold on to OSL Investment XIII, LLC for $17,500,000 (Kuttawa, +6.06%) and to OSL Investment XII, LLC together with Ohio State Life Insurance Company for $24,500,000 (Stardust, +4.26%) - $42,000,000 combined, +5.00%, all between affiliated parties - and then contributed up through OSL Marina II Holdings and OSL Marina II Investment Co into the Parent Trust on 24 August 2026. The contribution fee of $840,000 is charged on top, at exactly 2.00% of the $42,000,000. Against the original third-party price the offering is +22.42%. Small Bay III (row 18) shows the same shape: a $1,650,000 affiliate mark-up on Arapaho plus a 2.00% facilitation fee. Ask what the affiliates’ carrying costs were over those six months and why the $2,000,000 is not disclosed as sponsor compensation. And this PPM settles a question left open by the others: it defines “OSL” as Ohio State Life Insurance Company, confirming that the OSL entities running through Marina I, Lodging II and Small Bay III are Ohio State Life vehicles - the B+ (am Best) insurer disclosed in the Lodging II PPM as indirectly controlled by the same trust that controls NexPoint.

$646,400 of the early distributions is funded from the Investors’ own Offering proceeds, and it is concentrated in year 1. The $650,000 CapEx Reserve comes out of Offering Proceeds, and footnote 1 says so plainly: “No recurring capital expenditures are proposed for years 1-3 as the expenditures are funded through the initial CapEx reserve placed at closing.” Testing distributions against NOI less all capital spending less the Master Tenant’s income less DST expenses and the asset management fee: years 4 through 10 balance to the dollar, and years 1-3 are short by exactly $586,301, $34,300 and $25,800 - a cumulative $646,399 against $646,400 of Value-Add CapEx spend. Because Marina II front-loads that spend into year 1 (Marina I spread it over three years), the year 1 effect is much larger: 6.70% restates to 5.50%, down 1.20 points, against Marina I’s 0.68. Years 2 and 3 are negligible at -0.07 and -0.05 points. The 7.207% ten-year average is unaffected in substance, but the headline year-1 number is the softest part of this forecast.

The asset management fee caps the additional rent tier flat - the fourth NexPoint Offering in a row. “Additional Rent Maximum” runs $2,412,000 / $2,412,000 / $2,454,000 / $2,517,000 x 4 / $2,538,000 x 3 and the Asset Management Fee runs $0 / $0 / $42,000 / $105,000 x 4 / $126,000 x 3. In all ten years the Maximum equals $2,412,000 plus the fee exactly, so Additional Rent reaching investors is constant at $2,412,000 = 4.9257% of equity for the whole hold. Marina I does this at $2,214,000, Oasis at $1,748,000 and Small Bay III at $1,260,000. Four for four - read the Additional Rent line as a fee schedule, not a rent forecast. Growth from 6.70% to 8.00% comes from the Supplemental Rent tier (Master Tenant 10% of revenue above a breakpoint, Trust 90%) and from Base Rent. And the broken tax-equivalent-yield row recurs - but this time it understates. As in Marina I, “Yield Net of Tax Benefit” equals estimated taxable income x 1.37 in all ten years rather than distributions less tax. All-cash, so taxable income is positive throughout ($1,653,149 rising to $2,291,651) and the template built for a taxable loss misfires. Restated properly, the Effective Tax Equivalent Yield is higher than printed in years 1-9 - 8.65% against 7.34% in year 1, a 1.31-point understatement - and marginally lower only in year 10 (9.95% against 10.18%). Ten-year average 9.16% restated against 8.45% printed. In Marina I the identical error overstated by up to 3.11 points. Same formula, opposite direction, which is the clearest evidence that this is a broken row rather than a promotional choice. The rest of the tax chain is exact. For a non-1031 buyer: roughly 50% of the year 1 distribution is taxable ($1,653,149 of $3,279,463). Not tax advice. Everything else foots: all three fee percentages, the $44,389,504 of proceeds available, the $900,000 of reserves ($650,000 CapEx + $250,000 DST working capital), every chain identity and all ten cash-on-cash percentages. Front-end load 11.0654% of equity, essentially identical to Marina I’s 11.0358%. Cover-page error: “Maximum Offering Amount: $48,968,013 of Interests (0.204% ownership of the Trust)” - that should read 100%; 0.204% is the minimum-purchase percentage, and Marina I’s cover page reads “100%” correctly. The document is marked final.

name: NexPoint Oasis DST
lender: Berkeley Point Capital LLC d/b/a Newmark / Freddie Mac
amort: None - full-term interest-only. The entire $52,350,000 is a balloon at maturity 11/1/2035.
description:
NexPoint Oasis DST owns The Oasis at Shingle Creek, a garden-style multifamily community at 4350 Osceola Trail Road, Kissimmee, Florida, in the Orlando MSA. Developed in 2018: 27.35 acres, 15 residential buildings, 356 apartment units totalling approximately 347,081 rentable square feet at an average 975 SF per unit. 94.1% leased as of 22 July 2025.

Amenities include a resident lounge with game room, fitness centre, theatre, pool with private cabanas, indoor dog washing and grooming station, pet park with agility equipment, playground, sand volleyball court and a lakeside pier.

The Property is master-leased to NexPoint Oasis Leaseco, LLC, a sponsor affiliate, which subleases the units to residents. Day-to-day management is by BH Management Services, LLC - one of the fifteen largest apartment managers in the United States, with more than 85,000 units under management - which is described as providing services to the Sponsor, so treat it as a related operating relationship rather than a wholly independent one.
notes: The property provides a newer, high-occupancy Orlando multifamily profile but pairs it with 53.1% IO leverage and a ten-year balloon, which concentrates refinancing and exit risk in a single date and leaves the position exposed to cap-rate expansion. The property was acquired below its appraised value. The Master Tenant is a newly formed NexPoint affiliate funded with $250,000 of working capital; its rent obligation shifts operational cash flow but does not remove leasing, insurance, property tax and hurricane risk.
addresses: 4350 Osceola Trail Road, Kissimmee, FL 34746 (The Oasis at Shingle Creek - 356 units, ~347,081 RSF, 15 buildings on 27.35 acres, built 2018)
sourceNotes: All disclosures and source notes for this offering are carried in the Highlight 1-5 columns and in the 721 Exit column of this row. exit721Route: The only NexPoint offering here that names the receiving vehicle. The Operating Partnership is identified as NexPoint Diversified Real Estate Trust Operating Partnership, L.P. - the operating partnership of NXDT, a NYSE-listed REIT. It “may require that the Purchasers exchange their Interests for the OP Units,” and a Purchaser “may, however, elect to have the Operating Partnership purchase its Interests for cash in an amount equal to the then fair market value.” 90-day no-shop once the Notice of Exchange goes out; fair market value by an independent appraisal the Manager selects; facilitation fees up to 4.0% of the investment. Cash route: a genuine election and the default on silence - a Purchaser who fails to respond or will not sign “will not be admitted as a limited partner to the Operating Partnership and its Interests will be acquired for cash.” No cash cap and no redemption fee, which is better than Cantor Fitzgerald’s 5% cap and 1% fee. But NXDT is not NXRT. NexPoint’s two realised 721s (NREA Adair, NREA Estates) went into the operating partnership of NXRT, the listed multifamily REIT, at 1.70x and 2.00x. This offering points at NXDT - the former closed-end fund NexPoint Strategic Opportunities Fund / NHF, which converted to a diversified REIT in 2022 and is a different vehicle with a different asset mix and a different trading history. Before advising on a Units-versus-cash election here, check where NXDT shares trade relative to stated NAV, because that ratio is what an investor would be accepting. Do not carry NXRT’s record across to it.
highlights: The cleanest exhibit of any NexPoint offering in this workbook, and the headline matches the forecast. The Investment Summary’s “Annualized Cash on Cash Return 4.36%” and “Net Cash Flow $2,018,446” are exactly the forecast’s year 1 figures - no gap at all, in pointed contrast to NexPoint Life Sciences III where the same box overstates year 1 by 2.63 points. Every identity in the ten-year forecast reconciles to within $1: effective gross revenue less expenses equals NOI; Additional Rent less the asset management fee equals Additional Rent cash flow; Supplemental Rent plus the reserve contribution equals Supplemental cash flow; and Additional plus Supplemental cash flow equals Total Cash Flow in all ten years. The expense build foots line by line, and cumulative distributions tie exactly to the printed $10,458,197 through $22,771,853. The corollary is structural: base rent nets the Trust nothing - it exactly covers debt service plus the Master Tenant’s base income - so 100% of investor cash flow comes from the Additional and Supplemental Rent tiers.

Debt service proves out on ACTUAL/360, which confirms both the rate and the principal. $52,350,000 at 4.85% fixed, full-term interest-only with no amortisation, 120 months to 1 November 2035, from Berkeley Point Capital LLC d/b/a Newmark under the Freddie Mac Capital Markets Execution programme, non-recourse. A 30/360 calculation gives $2,538,975 a year, but the exhibit prints $2,574,239 - and $52,350,000 x 4.85% x 365/360 = $2,574,239 to the dollar, while the two years that print $2,581,291 are the leap years at 366/360. Eight years match 365/360 and years 3 and 7 match 366/360, exactly. Loan-to-capitalisation 53.0495%, confirmed independently from the minimum purchase ($112,990 of attributed debt against $212,990 of total cost = 53.0494%). The loan is interest-only for its whole life, so the entire $52,350,000 is a balloon at maturity - the forecast ends in year 10 with the balance unchanged and shows no refinancing or sale.

The asset management fee absorbs 100% of additional rent growth, so that tier is flat for ten years. Additional Rent rises from $1,748,000 to $2,140,625 across the forecast, and in every one of the ten years the asset management fee equals the difference exactly - leaving the Additional Rent reaching investors constant at $1,748,000 = 3.7728% of equity. The fee rate is not the “0.30%” the column label shows either: measured against the $87,250,000 purchase price it runs 0%, 0.150%, 0.300%, then 0.375% for years 4-7, 0.450% in year 8, and 0.300% in years 9-10 - understated in five of ten years by the printed rate, and footnote 2 says the fee “may be deferred or waived at the sole discretion of the Asset Manager,” which means the upside on this tier accrues to the Sponsor unless it chooses otherwise. All of the investor’s growth from 4.36% to 5.95% therefore comes from the Supplemental Rent tier, where the Master Tenant takes 10% of revenue above a breakpoint and the Trust takes 90%. NexPoint Marina does the identical thing at $2,214,000 - this is a feature of the sponsor’s master lease, not a one-off.

The 27.5-year depreciation life is correct here - and that is why the Life Sciences III version is wrong. This PPM says “the building allocation amount is depreciated over 27.5 years,” which is exactly right for residential rental property, and it does not claim that land is depreciated. The NexPoint Life Sciences III PPM applies the same 27.5-year life to a nonresidential medical-device R&D building (39 years) and adds that “the land is depreciated annually according to” MACRS; the NexPoint Marina PPM, drafted latest, gets it fully right - “39-year straight-line depreciation for nonresidential real property” and “land is not depreciable or amortizable.” Three versions of one paragraph across three PPMs, and only Life Sciences III is wrong. Here the building and land allocation ($78,488,013 and $10,911,987) sums to exactly the $89,400,000 appraised value, and the whole tax chain ties to the dollar in all ten years, with the Effective Tax Equivalent Yield running 8.24% to 9.84% on a genuine depreciation loss. Not tax advice.

Pricing, and the one small print error. Acquired 25 September 2025 from Shingle Creek Acquisition LLC, an unaffiliated third party, under a contract NexPoint Acquisitions LLC signed at $87,250,000 on 7 August 2025 and assigned to the Trust. Cooper Valuation & Advisory appraised the Property at $89,400,000 “as is” on 23 July 2025, so the purchase was 2.40% below appraisal; the $98,681,389 offering price is 10.38% above appraisal and 13.10% above the purchase price. The Sponsor discloses the dilution itself: the PPM states that the “net aggregate purchase price of $91,733,700 … is lower than the $98,681,389 aggregate purchase price of the Interests” and that “the Trust will be subject to immediate” dilution - and that $91,733,700 reconciles exactly as purchase price plus loan costs, the facilitation fee and other closing costs ($4,483,700), excluding reserves. On that basis the premium is +7.57%. The Facilitation Fee of $1,308,750 is exactly 1.500% of purchase price; front-end load is 12.17% of equity, the heaviest of the three NexPoint offerings reviewed together. Every cross-foot is exact: equity down payment $41,999,404 plus loan down payment $45,250,596 equals $87,250,000, and the loan side sums to $52,350,000. Print error: the comparable-sales table shows the subject at $251.28 per square foot, but $87,250,000 over 347,081 SF is $251.38 - a transposed digit. The per-unit figure of $245,084 is exactly right, which is what confirms the inputs are fine and only the printed PSF is wrong. It matters slightly because the comparable set averages $250.80, so the subject is marginally above the comps, not below. Separately the box prints a 4.84% capitalisation rate directly beneath “Offering Price $98,681,389”: 4.84% is NOI over offering price less the $2,615,704 of reserves ($96,065,685); on the offering price actually printed the cap rate is 4.71%.

NexPoint Small Bay III DST is a Parent Trust owning 100% of the Class 2 Beneficial Interests in two Operating Trusts, each holding one multi-tenant small-bay warehouse and industrial park - facilities the PPM describes as “typically smaller in size than standard facilities.” 177 units and approximately 509,914 net rentable square feet across roughly 39.8 acres.

exit721Route: Sponsor-side right, and the exchange entity is defined by the loan documents rather than by the Sponsor. Beneficial Owners grant the “Exchange Entity” - “the Manager, its affiliates, successors, or assigns who shall be controlled (as defined in the Loan Documents) by a key principal (as defined in the Loan Documents) or a wholly-owned Affiliate of such Key Principal” - the right, but not the obligation, to require each Beneficial Owner to exchange for units or to have their Interests purchased for cash. That is a fourth distinct formulation across four NexPoint offerings: Oasis names NXDT’s operating partnership, Life Sciences III says “Controlled by NexPoint,” Marina says only “affiliates, successors, or assigns,” and this one borrows the lender’s definition. Like Marina, and unlike the other two: “The Exchange Entity may exercise its Exchange Right at the Parent Trust level or at the Operating Trust level” - so it can take Arapaho and leave Deerfield, or the reverse, with value set by the sum of the fair market values of whichever Operating Trusts are taken. Cash route: available as an election. A Periodic Purchase Offer may also be extended after the second anniversary of the Acquisition Closings, entirely at the Sponsor’s discretion.
highlights: A Sponsor affiliate bought the Arapaho Property four months earlier and sold it to the Trust at a $1,650,000 mark-up. The chain is disclosed in full and is worth reading twice. Basis Industrial Acquisitions, LLC - an affiliate of the Property Manager - went under contract on 21 February 2025. On 24 April 2025 Basis assigned the purchase right to OSL Investment II, IV and V, LLC, and the PPM states plainly “OSL is an affiliate of the Sponsor.” On 1 May 2025 OSL acquired the Arapaho Property for $40,050,000 with cash. On 4 September 2025 the Arapaho DST acquired it from OSL for $41,700,000 - a $1,650,000 spread, +4.12%, in four months, captured by a sponsor affiliate and paid by the investors. The consideration was not cash: NREA SB III Holdings, LLC issued membership interests in Holdings to OSL. And the facilitation fee is charged on top - $1,434,000, exactly 2.00% of the $71,700,000 combined purchase price, so the Sponsor group is paid twice on the same acquisition. Separately, the Deerfield seller was WMG Deerfield Small Bay Owner, LLC, “an affiliate of the Property Manager” - so one property came from the sponsor’s own affiliate and the other from the manager’s. Neither purchase was arm’s length at the point the Trust bought. Ask what OSL’s carrying costs were over those four months, and why the $1,650,000 is not disclosed as sponsor compensation in the fee table.

Two footing problems in the use-of-proceeds table, one of which is a provable transposed digit. First: the loan column’s six line items sum to $40,982,000 against a printed total of $41,000,000 - $18,000 missing. Both reserve lines foot exactly to their own footnotes (lender reserves $200,000 + $836,561 + $522,789 + $408,281 + $4,500,000 = $6,467,631; trust reserves $200,000 + $1,250,000 + $489,776 = $1,939,776), so the error is not in the reserves. Solving for the down payment that makes the column foot gives $25,297,553 against the printed $25,279,553 - the digits 79 and 97 are transposed. Second, and not resolved by that fix: the combined down payment ($45,671,729 of equity plus the corrected $25,297,553 of loan) is $70,969,282 against a stated purchase price of $71,700,000 - short by $730,718, or 1.02%. Footnote (5) says the down payment is “exclusive of Loan-Related Costs and Other Closing Costs,” which means it should equal the price. The most ordinary explanation is closing prorations and credits, or the portion of the Arapaho price satisfied in Holdings membership interests rather than cash - but the PPM discloses neither, so this is a question for the Sponsor, not a conclusion. Everything else in the table is exact: all three fee percentages, the $45,671,729 of proceeds available, and the $91,382,493 total.

The headline overstates year 1 by exactly the DST expense line. The Investment Summary box prints “Net Cash Flow $2,356,549” and “Annualized Cash on Cash Return 4.68%,” while the Forecasted Statement of Cash Flows on the same exhibit prints Total Rent Paid to DST Investors of $2,326,549 and 4.62%. The difference is $30,000 - precisely the “DST Expenses” line the box omits. A 0.060-point gap, so far smaller than the 2.63 points at NexPoint Life Sciences III, but the same species of omission from the same template. Use 4.62%. Everything below the box reconciles: Base Rent plus Additional Rent plus the DST’s 90% of Supplemental Rent, less debt service, TI/LC replenishment, the asset management fee and DST expenses, equals Total Rent Paid to the dollar in all ten years, and all ten cash-on-cash percentages re-derive from dollars over equity.

The asset management fee caps the additional rent tier flat - the third NexPoint offering in a row to do this. Additional Rent runs $1,260,000 / $1,260,000 / $1,439,250 x 6 / $1,618,500 x 2, and the Asset Management Fee runs $0 / $0 / $179,250 x 6 / $358,500 x 2. In all ten years Additional Rent equals $1,260,000 plus the fee exactly, so the Additional Rent reaching investors is constant at $1,260,000 = 2.5009% of equity for the whole hold. NexPoint Oasis does the same at $1,748,000 (3.77%) and NexPoint Marina at $2,214,000 (5.18%). Three offerings, three different sponsors of the same master lease template, one identical mechanic - treat it as a structural feature, and read the Additional Rent line as a fee schedule rather than a rent forecast. Investor growth from 4.62% to 6.23% comes from the Supplemental Rent tier (Master Tenant 10% of revenue above a breakpoint, Trust 90%, which reconciles exactly) and from Base Rent. Note year 10 cash flow falls to 6.01% from 6.23%, driven by a $1,444,015 TI/LC reserve replenishment - the largest in the forecast.

Financing, pricing and the appraisal spread. $41,000,000 from Argentic Real Estate Finance 2 LLC at 5.708% fixed, 10-year term, full-term interest-only, non-recourse, with the two properties cross-collateralised - so a problem at one property can put the other at risk, which no other multi-property offering in this workbook does on a single loan. Debt service re-derives on ACTUAL/360: $41,000,000 x 5.708% x 365/360 = $2,372,784 and x 366/360 = $2,379,284, and the printed series uses the 366-day figure in years 1, 3 and 7. Years 3 and 7 are correct (the DST year begins 4 September 2025, so those years contain 29 February 2028 and 2032) but year 1 contains no 29 February and is overstated by $6,500 - conservative, understating year 1 cash-on-cash by 0.013 points. The loan never amortises, so the entire $41,000,000 balloons at maturity. LTC 44.8664%, confirmed from the minimum purchase ($81,377 of debt against $181,377 of total cost = 44.8662%) - the lowest leverage of the four leveraged NexPoint offerings. Pricing: Partner Valuation Advisors appraised Arapaho at $43,600,000 (3 October 2025) and Deerfield at $34,400,000 (6 October 2025), a combined $78,000,000 - so the $71,700,000 purchase was 8.08% below appraisal, the widest discount to appraisal in this workbook, and the $91,382,493 offering price is 17.16% above appraisal and 27.45% above the purchase price. Note both appraisals are dated after the 4 September 2025 closing. Front-end load 12.1962% of equity, the heaviest of the NexPoint set. Reserves are unusually large at $8,407,407 - 16.69% of equity - of which a $4,500,000 lender Rollover Reserve for tenant improvements and leasing commissions is the biggest single item, which is what a 177-unit multi-tenant industrial park with constant tenant turnover requires.

name: Resource Royalty 28, LLC
description:
Resource Royalty 28, LLC is not a Delaware Statutory Trust. It is an offering of undivided, non-possessory mineral Interests and non-participating royalty Interests in oil and gas properties, sold as “Direct-Title Units” at $100,000 each. Each investor receives a recorded mineral and royalty deed and becomes a co-owner of undivided interests alongside the other Interest Holders - there is no trust, no entity interest and no master lease. Resource Royalty 28, LLC is a Texas LLC formed 7 July 2026, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Resource Royalty, LLC, a Dallas oil and gas investment firm formed in 2010.

The portfolio: 14 deeded properties, 583.795 net royalty acres over 20,227 gross acres - an average royalty interest of 2.89% - across 7 counties in 2 states. Eleven properties sit in the Anadarko Basin of Oklahoma (STACK: Caddo, Canadian and Dewey Counties; SCOOP/Merge: Grady County; Western Anadarko: Custer County; Arkoma: Pittsburg County) and three in the Permian Basin of West Texas (Dawson County). 27 wells are currently producing, with 7 drilled-uncompleted, 2 drilling, 4 permitted, 17 filed to be drilled and 24 proven undeveloped locations. Operators named in the Executive Summary include Continental Resources, Flywheel Energy and Apache.

Zero debt. Quarterly distributions. Revenue runs from 1 July 2026 forward. The Royalties were acquired from unaffiliated companies, and only on private lands - the Offeror “will not use any of the funds of this offering for Royalties on state or federal lands,” which removes federal and state lease-renewal and permitting risk. Estimated remaining production life is “approximately 35 years, or more.”
addresses: 14 deeded properties, 583.795 net royalty acres over 20,227 gross acres (avg 2.89% royalty). OKLAHOMA (11 properties, Anadarko Basin): Caddo, Canadian and Dewey Cos (STACK); Grady Co (SCOOP/Merge); Custer Co (Western Anadarko); Pittsburg Co (Arkoma). TEXAS (3 properties, Permian Basin): Dawson Co. PRIVATE LANDS ONLY - no state or federal leases. NOTE: Exhibit A, the list of properties and legal descriptions, is NOT in the document.

Holding period: there is no fixed hold - each investor controls their own holding period and exit. The Sponsor targets 7-10 years for its own modelling only. exit721Route: No 721 mechanism exists, and none is needed - the Investor already controls the exit. There is no operating partnership, no REIT, no Exchange Entity, no FMV Option and no Code Section 721 anywhere in this offering. The word does not appear in the Memorandum. That is not an omission: this is not a DST. Each investor takes deeded direct title to undivided mineral and non-participating royalty interests and holds “the status of co-owner with respect to the other Interest Holders,” so there is nothing to exchange out of. And that is the structural advantage over every DST in this workbook. “With that deed in hand, investors are free to exercise control over holding period and exit strategy to suit their individual investment objectives” and “may sell or transfer their Royalties at any time.” The Management Agreement reinforces it: “the Manager shall not make any sale of any of the Interests without the prior written consent of interestholder.” No sponsor-controlled sale date, no 20-business-day election fuse, no cash cap, no springing LLC, no forced conversion into OP Units - and each owner can 1031 their own interest again on their own timetable. Compare Bluerock, where silence converts you into OP Units in 20 business days, or Brookfield, where the investor has no election at all. Cash route: there is only a cash route, by private sale of the investor’s own deeded interest. The cost of that freedom is liquidity: the PPM concedes there is “no formal market for fractional mineral interests and royalty interests,” the interests carry securities-law and USA PATRIOT Act transfer restrictions, and re-titling into another name or entity “may incur additional expenses.” Royalties are, however, giftable and inheritable as legacy assets.
types: Oil & Gas Royalties (mineral + NPRI) - not a DST
highlights: The 1031 position is better than the label suggests, but the support for it is not in the document. What is being sold is exactly the right thing: the PPM states that “the Offeror will only acquire Mineral and Non-Participating Royalty Interests,” both of which are perpetual interests in the mineral estate and therefore real property under Texas and Oklahoma law - and investors take deeded direct title as co-owners, not an interest in an LLC, which is what keeps the offering outside the partnership-interest exclusion in Code Section 1031(a)(2)(D). It deliberately excludes Overriding Royalty Interests, and the PPM itself explains why that matters: “courts have held that an Overriding Royalty Interest will terminate when the lease terminates.” (Do not be misled by the summary’s description of the Parent Company as a firm specialising in “Mineral Interests, Royalty Interests and/or Overriding Royalty Interests” - that describes the firm’s general business, not this fund’s holdings.) So far so good. The problem is the evidence. The cover page says “the Offeror has secured a tax opinion that an undivided interest in the Royalties should be treated as real property for purposes of a Section 1031 Exchange” - and that opinion is not attached, not summarised, and its author, date and assumptions are not disclosed. Worse, the Memorandum’s substantive tax section (“Federal Tax Consequences”) contains no Section 1031 discussion at all: it covers only royalty income characterisation and depletion. The string “1031” appears on the cover page and once more as an exhibit heading (“Qualified Intermediary Information for 1031 Purchasers”) and nowhere else in 108 pages - no like-kind analysis, no citation to the Section 1031 real-property regulations, no state-law title analysis. Get the opinion in writing before placing an exchange. Not tax advice.

Exhibit A - the list of the Properties being deeded - is missing from the document. The Memorandum directs the reader to Exhibit A nine separate times: for the properties themselves, for the wells in pay status, for the “several mineral interests” to which title will be deeded, and for the type-curve analysis. The section actually headed “overview of the Properties in this Offering” consists of one line: “See ‘Asset Listing’ in Exhibit A for detailed well listing, property legal descriptions, and other relevant information.” Exhibit A is listed in the table of contents as “List of Properties” - and it is not in the file, which is itself named “with exhibits.” Exhibits B, C and D (subscription agreement, company agreement, management agreement) are all present; the document ends with Exhibit D’s notary blocks. A search of all 108 pages returns zero township-and-range references, zero legal descriptions, zero well names and zero API numbers. Only the Executive Summary - explicitly marketing material that “must be accompanied by” the PPM - names three of the fourteen properties (Tiny Dancer and Ratliff in Grady County OK, Union Valley in Dawson County TX). An Investor taking deeded title cannot identify from this document which Interests they are buying, which for a 45-day replacement-property identification is not an academic problem. Request Exhibit A before anything else.

The prior performance section contains no data - not one number - for a Sponsor with 27 prior funds and $204 million raised. The Memorandum has a titled section, “prior performance of affiliates of the Parent Company,” and it runs to roughly 1,076 characters, all of which are disclaimer: what the information “represents,” that it “is not a prediction or projection,” that investors “should not assume that they will experience financial returns … comparable” - and then the section ends and the next heading begins. No table, no realised returns, no distribution history, no full-cycle results, nothing. The summary elsewhere states that “Resource Royalty or an affiliate has formed and managed twenty-seven investment funds and raised approximately $204,000,000,” deployed into “492 properties covering in excess of 506,000 gross acres in 5 states.” Sixteen years of operating history and none of it is disclosed. This is the largest prior-performance gap of any offering in this workbook - worse than Brookfield/BREX, which at least states plainly that it has no full-cycle record and why. Ask for realised distribution and disposition results on Funds 1 through 27 before recommending Fund 28.

The price deck, decoded - conservative for five years, then aggressive for thirty. The Supplement’s “Base Range” holds oil at $68.00, gas at $3.25, Oklahoma NGLs at $19.72 and Texas NGLs at $17.00 flat across all five forecast years, and the same Supplement prints the 27 July 2026 NYMEX strip beside it. Testing one against the other: the Base Range is the 2028 strip, flat-lined - oil $68.00 against a 2028 strip of $68.12, NGL-OK $19.72 against $19.75, NGL-TX $17.00 against $17.03, all within 0.2% - with gas haircut 9.5% below the 2028 strip ($3.25 against $3.59). The consequence is that the deck runs 4-7% below the strip in 2026-27 and 2-7% above it in 2029-30, while gas sits below the strip in every year from 2027. That is a defensible, mildly conservative construction. The terminal assumption is the one to challenge: the “to life” row - used to value everything beyond 2030, which for a 35-year-plus reserve life is most of the asset - holds oil at $73.21, gas at $3.04 and NGL-OK at $21.23 forever. That is the 2026 strip, i.e. the highest oil price on the entire table, held flat to life: 14.7% above the 2030 strip for oil and 14.8% above for NGLs (gas, at 13.4% below, is conservative). Oil and NGLs are the majority of SCOOP and Permian royalty revenue. Ask for the reserve report and for the sensitivity on a flat 2030 strip to life.

Distributions, fees and the numbers that do check out. The Supplement’s sensitivity analysis is the only distribution forecast - the PPM itself contains none - and it runs five years, not the seven to ten every DST in this workbook projects, against an asset with a stated 35-year-plus life. Base range: 8.00% in 2026 then 10.00% a year through 2030, cumulative 48.00%. Low range (oil $22.00, gas $1.50): 1.93% / 3.01% / 3.50% / 3.31% / 2.14%, cumulative 13.89% - so the downside case returns about a seventh of the base case over five years, and that is the honest measure of commodity exposure here. Both cumulative columns foot exactly to the sum of their annual figures. Read the 2026 figure carefully: it is footnoted “(8 mos of revenue)” yet the cumulative column adds the full 8.00 points, which implies a 12.00% annualised pace in the stub year falling to 10.00% thereafter.
